description: Width tiers for Languages — Background Language Learner Pathway, Years 3–4 band
subject: Languages — Background Language Learner

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest honest floor for the descriptor's command term at Y3-4. For communicating descriptors: the minimum range of task types or interaction contexts in which the capability has been demonstrated. For understanding descriptors: the minimum range of language features, text types or cultural contexts engaged with.
width_notes.typical_width: The full descriptor scope from ACARA elaborations — what a well-taught Y3-4 background language learner class would have engaged with.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions adding new task contexts (communicating) or new language/cultural phenomena (understanding). Background learners' home-language and community knowledge is a primary width resource at this band.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations for the Chinese Background Language Learner pathway (Y3-4) used as source data. Chinese-specific references are preserved as representative examples of the generic target-language principle.

AC9LCH4C01.minimum_width: Initiate at least one exchange by asking an opening question and sustain it for at least three turns; ask for clarification at least once using appropriate formulaic expressions; create at least one short interactive text (email, letter, or message) using appropriate format conventions.
AC9LCH4C01.typical_width: Initiate and sustain conversations about familiar topics — home, school, interests, daily routines; use turn-taking strategies; make suggestions; ask for clarification and seek help; create short texts in digital and written formats (emails, letters, messages, invitations) with appropriate conventions.
wider: Compare conversation initiation and digital communication conventions in the target language with English — identify differences in register, greeting, structure and sign-off
Initiate and sustain a conversation on a topic introduced unexpectedly by the partner — demonstrating flexibility in responding to an unplanned topic direction
Use emoticons and digital conventions to enhance meaning in a target language digital exchange, comparing their function with how they work in English digital communication
elaborations: initiating conversations by asking questions in different contexts using modelled responses
playing games where students take turns to role-play the teacher and give instructions
sharing information about themselves
participating in simple spoken exchanges with peers about familiar topics such as daily routines, local places or personal interests
initiating and maintaining communication by taking turns, for example, making suggestions
asking for clarification, using appropriate formulaic expressions and gestures
seeking advice and help from others
creating short texts such as emails, letters and text messages to interact with others
using emoticons in digital communication to enhance meaning

AC9LCH4C02.minimum_width: Participate in at least one transactional role-play using at least three appropriate target language phrases; contribute to planning at least one event or activity, making at least two planning decisions in target language.
AC9LCH4C02.typical_width: Participate in transactional scenarios — buying food, ordering, bargaining, planning itineraries; plan and present cultural items for school and community audiences; follow procedures and give instructions; interact with guest speakers; work in teams to create collaborative digital resources or games.
wider: Plan and lead a cultural presentation for a real audience — making decisions about content, assigning roles and directing the group using target language

Compare transactional and event-planning conventions in the target language community with Australian school conventions — identify cultural differences in etiquette, bargaining norms, and planning processes
Create a collaborative digital word or sentence game with peers and then lead the class through playing it
elaborations: planning and presenting a cultural item such as a festive occasion by reciting a poem, singing a song or performing a dance
performing plays with allocated roles within groups, using puppets and props
participating in group activities and role-plays involving scenarios such as buying food or ordering a meal
negotiating details in a transaction, such as stating preferred size, quantity or price
participating in traditional or contemporary games involving taking turns, active listening and information exchange
following procedures or giving modelled instructions
reading their own work to others
working in teams to create word or sentence games using digital applications
interacting with guest speakers or classroom visitors during special occasions
planning and discussing cultural items to present for a school event

AC9LCH4C03.minimum_width: Locate at least three key pieces of information in a familiar text and identify its main purpose; gather information from at least two sources and organise findings in a different format (timeline, graph, table, or summary).
AC9LCH4C03.typical_width: Locate and identify key words and information in spoken, written and multimodal texts; gather information from a range of sources including interviews; organise and present findings in new formats; retell and summarise texts; read aloud and recite with attention to pronunciation and intonation; create performances in response to legends and folk tales.
wider: Interview family members about languages spoken, country of origin, or participation in cultural events — present the information collected for a specific audience

Learn that First Nations Australian languages change according to connections and relationships between people, and investigate examples of how language variation also occurs within the target language community
Compare how information is organised and presented differently across two target language text types — for example, a folk tale versus an informative report
elaborations: watching educational television programs, listening to songs or playing digital games, and sharing personal opinions
identifying and locating familiar characters or words in texts and discussing main purpose and meaning
creating a timeline of the main events of a story using words, pictures or simple sentences
learning that First Nations Australian languages change according to connections and relationships between people, and giving examples of how this occurs in Chinese
gathering information from a range of sources and presenting findings in a different way
responding to words of songs through movement and dance
interviewing family, friends or peers about languages spoken, country of origin or cultural events
listening to, reading and viewing a range of informative and imaginative texts and retelling or summarising
reading aloud or reciting texts paying attention to pronunciation, intonation and emotion
creating performances in response to legends and folk tales using modelled language

AC9LCH4C04.minimum_width: Identify at least two contexts requiring different levels of formality in the target language and produce appropriate language for each; identify at least two expressions that do not translate directly into English and explain their cultural meaning; use a bilingual dictionary to locate at least three words selecting context-appropriate meanings.
AC9LCH4C04.typical_width: Distinguish formal and informal registers across social contexts; identify culturally-specific terms, colloquialisms and untranslatable expressions; explain the cultural value behind symbols and occasion-specific language; develop and use bilingual dictionary strategies; create bilingual resources for classroom use.
wider: Translate a short text containing idiomatic or culturally-embedded expressions, documenting each translation decision and explaining the strategy used
Compare culturally-specific terms and phrases across the target language and Australian English — share insights into why particular cultures value certain colloquial language
Research the cultural value behind a specific symbol used in the target language community — explain what the symbol means and why particular language is associated with it
elaborations: selecting language to translate information, recognising different meanings for the same word
demonstrating levels of politeness, respect and formality in diverse contexts
explaining when to use formal and informal language in different social contexts
recognising the role that gesture plays in interactions, including taboos within target language communication
creating bilingual resources for use in the classroom or school
identifying words and expressions in the target language and English that do not readily translate
developing strategies for using bilingual print or digital dictionaries
learning the cultural value behind symbols used in cultural events
identifying culturally-specific terms and phrases and sharing insights into why cultures value certain colloquial language

AC9LCH4C05.minimum_width: Create at least one informative text with at least five target language sentences and appropriate textual conventions; create and perform at least one imaginative text with a clear structure using at least six target language phrases.
AC9LCH4C05.typical_width: Create informative texts — visual displays, presentations, annotated posters, digital storyboards — about topics of personal or community interest; create and perform imaginative texts — alternative story endings, action songs, dialogues, plays; use a range of sentence structures with appropriate script conventions; create simple descriptions for real-world contexts including First Nations Country/Place connections.
wider: Create a text for a real external audience — a community newsletter, school publication, or bilingual display for Chinese-speaking families — with language and format selected for that audience
Create simple descriptions in the target language and match them to appropriate First Nations Country/Place locations in the local area or elsewhere in Australia
Create an original imaginative text not based on a familiar story — with a deliberate structural choice and at least one creative language decision
elaborations: presenting a visual display with supporting text on a topic of personal interest
supporting presentations using pictures, charts and graphs
conveying information about school and community events in written and multimodal texts
creating simple descriptions in Chinese and matching them to appropriate First Nations Country/Place locations
presenting a show and tell about an object, activity or person special to them
using familiar words, phrases or idioms to create raps or songs
creating alternative endings to familiar stories
creating and performing simple imaginative texts to share with teachers and peers
creating a mini-book relating to a familiar topic

AC9LCH4U01.minimum_width: Produce all tones with recognisable accuracy in at least five words and demonstrate awareness of at least one tone change rule; explain in simple terms what the phonetic system represents and identify at least two sounds that differ from English equivalents.
AC9LCH4U01.typical_width: Differentiate and produce the full tonal system including neutral tone; use hand gestures to demonstrate tone; read aloud and recite with attention to phrasing, stress and intonation; explain the phonetic system as a learning tool; match phonetic representations to syllables; identify diversity in spoken varieties and differences in phonology across dialects.
wider: Investigate diversity in spoken target language and identify differences in phonology across dialects — compare greetings in different dialects and discuss what the variation reveals about the language community
Record own speech and compare tonal accuracy with a standard model — identify specific tones that need attention and design a targeted practice plan
Research the relationship between the phonetic system and spoken standard target language — explain what the phonetic system captures and what its limitations are for learners
elaborations: reading aloud and reciting, focusing on phrasing, stress and intonation
engaging in activities to consolidate tonal awareness using hand gestures
differentiating the 4 tones when speaking and knowing when and how to use the neutral tone
explaining the use of Pinyin as a learning tool to reflect spoken sounds
playing pair-matching card games matching Pinyin to syllables
investigating diversity in spoken Chinese and identifying differences in phonology across dialects

AC9LCH4U02.minimum_width: Write at least five characters or script elements with correct stroke order; identify the components of at least three compound characters and explain how each component contributes to meaning; produce at least four sentences demonstrating at least three syntactic features.
AC9LCH4U02.typical_width: Apply stroke direction and order when writing; identify and categorise characters by shared components; build new words by mixing and matching components; use multiple sentence structures — statements, questions, sentences with modifiers, adverbs, prepositions; elaborate ideas in sentences with time, manner and place details; use writing conventions including text direction and punctuation.
wider: Investigate the types of character formation in the target language writing system and identify examples of each — explain the logic behind each formation type
Analyse a compound character and explain both its semantic component and phonetic component — then apply this knowledge to predict the meaning of a related unfamiliar character
Compare specific syntactic features — for example, how location prepositions work — in the target language and English, identifying where they behave similarly and where they differ
elaborations: using Chinese writing conventions including direction of text and punctuation
applying rules of stroke direction and stroke order when writing characters
making connections between basic characters and related component forms such as radicals
mixing and matching Chinese characters to make new meanings
categorising Chinese characters with common components and identifying connections
recognising that there are multiple ways to structure a sentence
using reduplication adjectives in sentences to describe people, animals and objects
using adverbs to modify actions
experimenting with the use of prepositions
recognising basic structures of closed and open-ended questions
elaborating ideas in sentences including details such as time, manner and place

AC9LCH4U03.minimum_width: Identify at least two features of different text genres in the target language and compare with English for at least one; use at least four metalanguage terms correctly in describing a grammar rule or comparison; identify at least two examples of English influence on everyday target language use.
AC9LCH4U03.typical_width: Recognise features of narratives, procedural and explanatory texts; compare features of the same genre across target language and English; use metalanguage to describe grammatical placement rules; identify similarities and differences in layout, script and organisation across text types; explore how English influences informal everyday target language use.
wider: Compare the same genre text in target language and English — identify all structural and language feature differences and discuss what they reveal about how genre conventions differ across the two languages
Research the history of specific borrowed words or code-switched expressions in everyday target language use — trace where they came from and identify patterns
Create a genre comparison guide for a peer explaining how to recognise a particular genre in both languages and what conventions must be followed
elaborations: using metalanguage to describe grammar rules
recognising language features and symbols typically associated with particular text types
identifying and comparing key words in target language and English versions of favourite stories
identifying and documenting similarities and differences in elements such as titles, layout, images and script of target language and English texts
exploring the influence of English on informal language used in daily interactions by target language speakers
recognising features of various genres and identifying which genres are most suitable for different purposes

AC9LCH4U04.minimum_width: Identify at least two target language expressions that encode cultural values or beliefs and explain what each reveals about the culture; identify at least two ways cultural identity is expressed through language in different target language communities or regions.
AC9LCH4U04.typical_width: Examine how feelings, beliefs and values are reflected in language; notice differences in cultural practices and protocols across events; identify locations of major dialect groups; explore how cultural identity is expressed through daily life, music, dance, and cultural performance; compare target language and Australian lifestyles.
wider: Explore representations of information used in cultural expressions of First Nations Australians and make connections with those of target language culture — compare differences in cultural expression forms and purposes

Investigate how music and dance serve as expressions of identity and emotion in the target language culture, identifying the language used in cultural performance contexts and what values it expresses
Compare how a specific cultural value is encoded in language differently across target language community contexts — diaspora, regional, and homeland — and discuss what the differences reveal
elaborations: understanding that feelings, beliefs and values can be reflected in language
noticing differences in cultural practices and the protocol for certain events
identifying locations of major dialect groups in target language speaking countries and regions
exploring representations of information used in cultural expressions of First Nations Australians and making connections with those of Chinese language and culture
identifying ways in which their Chinese identity is reflected in their daily life and interests
participating in cultural practices and discussing their cultural significance
comparing Chinese and Australian lifestyles, festivals and celebrations
experiencing and discussing the importance of music and dance as an expression of identity and emotion
recognising characters used in specific cultural events and how the form might change across contexts
